power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Alcohol use contributes to injury, making trauma care an opportunity to address harmful drinking.
In Tanzania, the Punguza Pombe Kwa Afya Yako (PPKAY) brief intervention reduced binge-drinking days among trauma patients at three months.
However, its overall effect does not establish whether patients with different patterns of alcohol-related harms respond differently.
Aims: To identify baseline profiles of risky alcohol-related behaviours and assess whether PPKAY effectiveness differed across profiles.
We analysed data from a pragmatic randomised adaptive trial at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre (2020-2025).
Latent class analysis of ten Drinker Inventory of Consequences indicators included 674 patients.
Classification-error-adjusted regression examined profile characteristics.
Among 543 patients with recorded three-month follow-up, baseline-adjusted models compared pooled PPKAY arms with usual care and tested intervention-by-profile interactions.
Binge-drinking days was the primary outcome; bootstrap-then-impute procedures estimated confidence intervals.
Results: Two profiles were identified: lower-risk with driving-related harms (531; 78.8%) and pervasive high-risk behaviours (143; 21.2%).
Younger age, higher alcohol-use severity, depressive symptoms and perceived injury severity characterised the high-risk profile.
For binge-drinking days, PPKAY incidence rate ratios were 0.84 (95% CI 0.22-3.37) and 0.023 (95% CI 0.001-0.223), respectively.
The interaction ratio was 0.028 (95% CI 0.001-0.456; p = 0.024).
Interactions for drinking days and drinking amount were not statistically significant.
Conclusions: PPKAY had a stronger estimated effect on binge-drinking days in the pervasive highrisk profile.

PPKAY should remain available to all eligible trauma patients, while broader assessment of alcohol-related harms and depressive symptoms should be evaluated to identify patients needing additional support.
Alcohol contributed to an estimated 2.6 million deaths worldwide in 2019, including approximately 700,000 deaths from injuries (World Health Organization, 2024).

text.text: Its contribution to trauma is evident in northern Tanzania.

At Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre (KCMC), 30.0% of adult injury patients tested positive for alcohol at presentation, and alcohol use during the six hours before injury was associated with higher odds of injury (odds ratio 5.71) (Staton et al., 2018).

text.text: We used the broader 2020-2025 PRACT cohort to identify and characterise baseline profiles of risky alcohol-related behaviours among adult trauma patients at KCMC.
We then assessed whether the three-month PPKAY effect differed across the profiles.
The number of binge-drinking days was the primary effectiveness outcome; drinking days and total drinking amount were secondary outcomes.
PRACT was conducted at KCMC, a zonal referral and teaching hospital in Moshi, northern Tanzania.
Research staff identified potentially eligible patients through the Emergency Medicine Department.
For admitted patients, baseline assessment and intervention delivery could be completed in the inpatient ward.
Follow-up assessments were conducted by telephone after discharge.
The parent-trial protocol describes recruitment, allocation and intervention procedures (Staton et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The parent-trial protocol describes recruitment, allocation and intervention procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Staton et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The parent study was a three-stage adaptive randomised trial.
In Stage 1, participants were allocated in blocks of 12 to usual care, PPKAY with standard weekly text-message boosters, or PPKAY with personalised weekly boosters.
Later stages compared PPKAY-based conditions after usual care was removed.
The published Stage 1 report included participants recruited from 12 October 2020 to 14 April 2023 (Staton et al., 2022; Staton et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: The published Stage 1 report included participants recruited from 12 October 2020 to 14 April 2023 <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Staton et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Staton et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: All PPKAY conditions included a trained nurse's approximately 15-minute face-to-face discussion that raised the subject of alcohol, provided personalised feedback, explored motivation and negotiated drinking-reduction goals.
Booster conditions added weekly standard or personalised text messages.
Usual care comprised routine injury care without systematic alcohol counselling (Staton et al., 2022; Staton et al., 2025b).
text.formatted: Usual care comprised routine injury care without systematic alcohol counselling <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Staton et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Staton et al., 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Parent-trial eligibility required age of at least 18 years, presentation within 24 hours of acute injury, and at least one alcohol-risk criterion: reported alcohol use before injury, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) score of at least 8, or a positive breath-alcohol result.
Participants had to be clinically sober and able to consent and complete telephone follow-up.
Patients initially too ill or intoxicated were reassessed after stabilisation.
Exclusions included inability to communicate in Swahili, residence in East Africa for fewer than five years, no telephone access and imprisonment (Staton et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Exclusions included inability to communicate in Swahili, residence in East Africa for fewer than five years, no telephone access and imprisonment <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Staton et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We analysed participant-level data collected during 2020-2025.
The fixed baseline cohort comprised 674 participants, all with at least seven of the ten selected DrInC indicators observed.
Baseline indicators were used to derive the classes before examining their associations with participant characteristics or intervention outcomes.
For effectiveness analyses, PPKAY conditions were pooled and compared with usual care using the original allocation.
One participant lacked recorded allocation.
The effectiveness sample comprised participants with recorded allocation and a threemonth assessment record.
No additional sample-size calculation was undertaken for this secondary analysis.
Reporting was guided by SMART-LCA and applicable STROBE and CONSORT items (von Elm et al., 2007; van Lissa et al., 2024; Hopewell et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Reporting was guided by SMART-LCA and applicable STROBE and CONSORT items <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(von Elm et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">van Lissa et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Hopewell et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The ten DrInC indicators assessed consequences during the preceding three months: driving after at least three drinks, greater use of other drugs, foolish risks, regretted impulsive acts, physical fights, increased smoking, becoming overweight, drink-driving arrest, legal problems and an accident while drinking or intoxicated.
Each had four response levels: never, once or a few times, once or twice a week, and daily or almost daily (Miller et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Each had four response levels: never, once or a few times, once or twice a week, and daily or almost daily <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Miller et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The same indicators had been used in the earlier Moshi analysis (Zhao et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The same indicators had been used in the earlier Moshi analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Zhao et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Alcohol outcomes were derived from Timeline Follow-Back records for the preceding 28 days (Sobell and Sobell, 1992).
text.formatted: Alcohol outcomes were derived from Timeline Follow-Back records for the preceding 28 days <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Sobell and Sobell, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: A binge-drinking day involved at least five standard drinks for men or four for women; one standard drink represented approximately 14 g of pure alcohol.
Drinking days counted days with any alcohol use, and drinking amount was the total number of standard drinks.

Baseline questionnaires also measured AUDIT over 12 months, depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) over two weeks (Kroenke et al., 2001), education, partnered status and participant-perceived injury severity.
text.formatted: Baseline questionnaires also measured AUDIT over 12 months, depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) over two weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kroenke et al., 2001)</ref>, education, partnered status and participant-perceived injury severity.

text.text: The five severity responses were grouped as less serious, neutral, or serious/life-threatening.
Research assistants blinded to allocation conducted the three-month telephone assessments (Staton et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: Research assistants blinded to allocation conducted the three-month telephone assessments <ref type="bibr">(Staton et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: We fitted exploratory one-to six-class models to the original four-level indicators using poLCA (Linzer and Lewis, 2011).
text.formatted: We fitted exploratory one-to six-class models to the original four-level indicators using poLCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Linzer and Lewis, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Each model used 100 random starts, a maximum of 5,000 iterations and seed 54123.
The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) received greatest weight in class selection.

We also considered the Akaike information criterion (AIC), entropy, posterior membership probabilities, minimum class size, convergence, replication of the maximum likelihood and clinical interpretability (Nylund et al., 2007; van Lissa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We also considered the Akaike information criterion (AIC), entropy, posterior membership probabilities, minimum class size, convergence, replication of the maximum likelihood and clinical interpretability <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Nylund et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Available indicator responses contributed to model estimation.
The selected model's item-response probabilities were summarised as the probability of any endorsement, defined as a response above zero.
Participants were assigned to the class with the highest posterior membership probability for descriptive and effectiveness analyses.
We assessed local independence using bivariate residuals and 500 simulated datasets, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across indicator pairs (Oberski et al., 2013).
text.formatted: We assessed local independence using bivariate residuals and 500 simulated datasets, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across indicator pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Oberski et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Robustness analyses repeated class estimation among participants with all ten indicators, those with at least eight indicators, and after omitting each indicator in turn.
An alternative three-class solution was also examined.
These checks assessed sensitivity to indicator availability, individual items and class count.
Continuous characteristics were summarised using means and standard deviations or medians and quartiles; categorical characteristics were summarised using counts and percentages.
Descriptive comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests and Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate.
Adjusted associations with profile membership were estimated using classification-erroradjusted three-step logistic regression (Vermunt, 2010; Bray et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Adjusted associations with profile membership were estimated using classification-erroradjusted three-step logistic regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Vermunt, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bray et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Covariates were age group (18-24, 25-34, 35-44 or at least 45 years), education years, partnered status, AUDIT category (0-7, 8-15, 16-19 or 20-40), PHQ-9 category (0-4, 5-9 or 10-27), and perceived injury severity.
This model used complete records for those variables.
We report adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals.
We fitted separate baseline-adjusted generalised linear models for each three-month alcohol outcome.
Each model contained study arm, profile, their interaction, age, baseline AUDIT score and the baseline value of the corresponding outcome.
Each participant contributed one follow-up observation.

A negative binomial type 2 distribution was used for binge-drinking days, a zero-inflated negative binomial type 2 distribution with an intercept-only zero-inflation component for drinking days, and a Tweedie distribution for drinking amount.
Candidate distributions were assessed on the same complete observed sample using AIC, BIC, convergence and diagnostics (Dunn and Smyth, 2005; Brooks et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Candidate distributions were assessed on the same complete observed sample using AIC, BIC, convergence and diagnostics <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dunn and Smyth, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Brooks et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For each outcome, we estimated the PPKAY effect within each profile and the ratio comparing those two effects.
Exponentiated coefficients are reported as incidence rate ratios for the count-model components and mean ratios for drinking amount.
Ratios below one indicate a lower adjusted outcome under PPKAY.
The binge-drinking-days interaction was the primary test; the other two interactions were secondary.
Tests were two-sided, with statistical significance assessed at p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Tests were two-sided, with statistical significance assessed at p < 0.05.

text.text: Analyses were conducted in R version 4.6.0.
We distinguished incomplete values within a recorded assessment from the absence of an assessment record.
Descriptive summaries used available observations.
A complete-record logistic model examined baseline factors associated with absent three-month follow-up.
In effectiveness analyses, incomplete numeric values were eligible for multiple imputation when the corresponding assessment record existed; absent three-month assessments were not imputed.
Original allocation, class assignment, assessment-record indicators and observed values were retained.

Multiple imputation by chained equations used predictive mean matching with five donors for eligible education, PHQ-9 and alcohol-outcome values (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011; Morris et al., 2014).

text.text: Predictors included baseline AUDIT and available alcohol measures from other assessments.
Imputation assumed that incomplete values were missing at random conditional on observed predictors (White et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Imputation assumed that incomplete values were missing at random conditional on observed predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(White et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The primary procedure drew 500 participant-level bootstrap samples within the four study-arm-by-profile groups.
Within each resample, two datasets were imputed using 20 iterations.
Models were fitted to both completed datasets and estimates averaged within each resample.
The final point estimate averaged the bootstrap estimates, and their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles formed the 95% confidence interval (Bartlett and Hughes, 2020).
text.formatted: The final point estimate averaged the bootstrap estimates, and their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles formed the 95% confidence interval <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bartlett and Hughes, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For sensitivity analysis, 100 datasets were imputed using 50 iterations and seed 54123, and model estimates were combined using Rubin's rules (Rubin, 1987).

text.text: Participants in the pervasive high-risk class were younger and had higher median AUDIT, PHQ-9 and DrInC scores than those in the lower-risk class (Table 1).
text.formatted: Participants in the pervasive high-risk class were younger and had higher median AUDIT, PHQ-9 and DrInC scores than those in the lower-risk class (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: In the adjusted model, participants aged at least 45 years had lower odds of pervasive high-risk membership than those aged 18-24 years (adjusted OR 0.193, 95% CI 0.063-0.587).
Compared with AUDIT scores of 0-7, adjusted odds ratios were 6.08 (95% CI 1.87-19.74) for scores of 16-19 and 14.63 (95% CI 4.78-44.77) for scores of at least 20.
Mild and moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were each associated with approximately fourfold higher odds.
Serious or life-threatening perceived injury severity was also associated with higher odds (adjusted OR 6.59, 95% CI 1.20-36.31).
Associations with education and partnered status were not statistically significant (Table 2).
text.formatted: Associations with education and partnered status were not statistically significant (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: For binge-drinking days, the adjusted PPKAY incidence rate ratio was 0.84 (95% CI 0.22-3.37) in the lower-risk class and 0.023 (95% CI 0.001-0.223) in the pervasive high-risk class.
Observed threemonth binge-drinking means were 1.3 days under usual care and 0.2 under PPKAY in the pervasive high-risk class, and 0.6 days in each arm in the lower-risk class.
The intervention-by-profile interaction ratio was 0.028 (95% CI 0.001-0.456; p = 0.024), indicating a stronger effect in the pervasive high-risk class.
Interactions for drinking days (ratio 0.428, 95% CI 0.132-1.392; p = 0.144) and drinking amount (ratio 0.308, 95% CI 0.080-1.415; p = 0.104) were not statistically significant (Table 3).

text.text: Two behavioural profiles described risky alcohol-related consequences among adult trauma patients at KCMC.
Most participants belonged to a lower-risk class in which driving-related harms remained prominent.

The smaller pervasive high-risk class reported consequences across several behavioural domains and was characterised by younger age, greater alcohol-use severity, depressive symptoms and higher perceived injury severity.
Among participants with recorded three-month follow-up, PPKAY had a stronger effect on binge-drinking days in the pervasive high-risk class.
The interactions for drinking days and drinking amount were not statistically significant.
The earlier Moshi study used the same ten indicators and identified three profiles among community and injury participants (Zhao et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The earlier Moshi study used the same ten indicators and identified three profiles among community and injury participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Zhao et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: United States trauma studies identified five classes in the original analysis and four in a replication using seven consequence indicators (Cochran et al., 2014; Cochran et al., 2016a).
text.formatted: United States trauma studies identified five classes in the original analysis and four in a replication using seven consequence indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cochran et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cochran et al., 2016a)</ref>.

text.text: Each study identified a group with consequences across several domains.
The studies differed in their populations, indicators and criteria for choosing the number of classes.
The current cohort comprised injured adults meeting alcohol-risk eligibility criteria and was predominantly male.
Driving-related consequences deserve attention within the lower-risk class.
About one-quarter endorsed driving after three or more drinks, and a similar proportion endorsed an accident while drinking or intoxicated.
The accident item did not specify accident type.
Asking about these behaviours during brief intervention can help nurses discuss specific goals, such as avoiding driving after drinking, even with patients who report fewer consequences overall.
Alcohol-use severity and depressive symptoms were independently associated with pervasive highrisk membership.
The relationship with AUDIT is consistent with the earlier Moshi finding that broader risky behaviours accompanied heavier alcohol use (Zhao et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The relationship with AUDIT is consistent with the earlier Moshi finding that broader risky behaviours accompanied heavier alcohol use <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Zhao et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The association with perceived injury severity also supports discussing the patient's experience of the injury during alcohol counselling.
These findings support assessment of depressive symptoms alongside alcohol use and behavioural consequences.
The binge-drinking-days interaction extends the overall PPKAY trial finding by identifying variation across behavioural profiles.
The pervasive high-risk estimate corresponded to a 97.7% lower adjusted number of binge-drinking days under PPKAY than under usual care.
Its direction is consistent with the trauma analysis in which multiple-risk and injury/drink-driving classes showed greater improvement following brief intervention (Cochran et al., 2016b).
text.formatted: Its direction is consistent with the trauma analysis in which multiple-risk and injury/drink-driving classes showed greater improvement following brief intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cochran et al., 2016b)</ref>.

text.text: Profile-dependent responses have also been reported among young adults receiving motivational interviewing or brief advice (Gaume et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Profile-dependent responses have also been reported among young adults receiving motivational interviewing or brief advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gaume et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, an East African trial among people living with HIV found weaker alcoholcounselling effects among participants with higher baseline alcohol biomarker levels (Puryear et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In contrast, an East African trial among people living with HIV found weaker alcoholcounselling effects among participants with higher baseline alcohol biomarker levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Puryear et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These comparisons involved different clinical populations and definitions of baseline risk, including behavioural consequences and alcohol biomarker levels.
Greater baseline binge drinking and a broader range of consequences in the pervasive high-risk class provided more opportunity for improvement.
Personalised feedback and negotiated goals may have been particularly relevant to these patients (Staton et al., 2025b).
text.formatted: Personalised feedback and negotiated goals may have been particularly relevant to these patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Staton et al., 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Prospective studies can examine whether motivation to change, injury attribution or engagement accounts for this difference.
Bingedrinking days reflect high-intensity episodes; drinking days and total amount describe frequency and volume.

Primary-care integration work in Tanzania has introduced screening, provider training and referral arrangements (Mushi et al., 2024), while PPKAY provides a culturally adapted brief intervention within trauma care (Staton et al., 2025b).
text.formatted: Primary-care integration work in Tanzania has introduced screening, provider training and referral arrangements <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mushi et al., 2024)</ref>, while PPKAY provides a culturally adapted brief intervention within trauma care <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Staton et al., 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Continued PPKAY delivery can be combined with prospective evaluation of additional support for patients reporting pervasive harms.
Such studies can assess whether adding behavioural assessment helps nurses set counselling goals and identify patients who need further care.

Strengths include a locally delivered intervention, behavioural indicators previously studied in Moshi, retention of all 674 participants in class derivation, classification-error adjustment for profile associations, formal interaction testing and sensitivity analyses.
Agreement across the primary and Rubin-pooled procedures supports the stability of the binge-drinking interaction across these two methods.
The parent trial was powered for its overall treatment effect.
The pervasive high-risk usual-care subgroup contained 37 participants at baseline, and its size contributed to imprecision.
PPKAY conditions were pooled across trial stages, whereas usual care was confined to Stage 1; calendarperiod differences could therefore contribute to the comparison.
A recorded three-month assessment was absent for 19.3% of participants with allocation.
Because their outcomes were not imputed, selection bias is possible if follow-up depended on unobserved alcohol outcomes.
These features are relevant when interpreting this secondary interaction analysis (Sun et al., 2012).
text.formatted: These features are relevant when interpreting this secondary interaction analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Sun et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Eleven indicator pairs showed residual dependence, and omission of some indicators altered classification.
The class-enumeration procedure did not include likelihood-ratio tests.
Effectiveness models treated modal class assignments as fixed, so their intervals did not include uncertainty from deriving or assigning the profiles (Bray et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Effectiveness models treated modal class assignments as fixed, so their intervals did not include uncertainty from deriving or assigning the profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bray et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Imputation within recorded assessments assumed missing at random, and two imputations per bootstrap sample may affect percentile-interval precision (White et al., 2011; Bartlett and Hughes, 2020).
text.formatted: Imputation within recorded assessments assumed missing at random, and two imputations per bootstrap sample may affect percentile-interval precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(White et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bartlett and Hughes, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the single-hospital, predominantly male sample and self-reported measures define the setting for interpretation.
Independent validation and concurrent comparisons would strengthen evaluation of the profiles in clinical practice.
Two profiles distinguished lower-risk with driving-related harms from pervasive high-risk behaviours among Tanzanian trauma patients.
PPKAY had a stronger three-month effect on binge-drinking days in the pervasive high-risk profile.
Interactions for drinking days and drinking amount were not statistically significant.
The findings support assessment of behavioural consequences alongside alcohol consumption and depressive symptoms, and further evaluation of tailored support within trauma-based alcohol care.

We used de-identified data, with no additional participant contact.
All 674 participants contributed to class derivation.
Mean age was 36.5 years (SD 12.7), and 631 (93.6%) were male.
Recorded allocation was available for 673 participants: 171 usual care and 502 pooled PPKAY.
Three-month follow-up was recorded for 543 (80.7%), including 142 usual-care and 401 PPKAY participants.
Of these, 508 had complete values for all three outcomes and 35 had incomplete values addressed by imputation.
The remaining 130 participants had no three-month assessment record.
Adjusted profile characterisation included 646 complete records (Figure 1; Supplementary Tables S2-S3).

text.text: The two-class solution had the lowest BIC (7274.4), entropy of 0.816, and a smallest class of 143 participants.
Its maximum likelihood was reproduced in 46 of 100 starts.
The four-class solution had a lower AIC but only 20 participants in its smallest class and reproduced its maximum likelihood in one start (Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: The selected classes were lower-risk with driving-related harms (531; 78.8%) and pervasive high-risk behaviours (143; 21.2%).
Mean posterior probabilities for assigned membership were 0.963 and 0.898, respectively.
In the lower-risk class, driving after three or more drinks (24.3%), an accident while drinking or intoxicated (23.2%) and increased smoking (17.5%) had the highest endorsement probabilities.
The pervasive high-risk class had higher probabilities across all ten indicators.
Its most prominent behaviours were regretted impulsive acts (73.9%), foolish risks (68.5%), the accident item (54.7%) and driving after three or more drinks (53.5%) (Figure 2).
